title: Chapter 5: The Intractable 3
content:
Chapter 5

The Lan disciples were greenhorns out on the field for the first time. Every face was taut with nerves, yet they moved with crisp discipline, locking down the compound's perimeter according to precise formations and slapping talismans across every door and lintel. Inside the Eastern Hall, the servant A-Tong had been hauled in and laid flat on the floorboards. Lan Sizhui sat wedged between two crises: his left hand pressed to A-Tong’s wrist checking for a pulse, his right channeling spiritual energy into Madam Mo’s back to steady her failing breath. He was burning the candle at both ends, running out of options fast, when A-Tong suddenly lurched upright.

A-Ding let out a gasp. “A-Tong! You’re awake!”

The relief died in her throat before it could even reach her eyes.

A-Tong raised his left hand, reached across, and clamped it viciously around his own throat.

Lan Sizhui reacted instantly, striking three acupoints along the boy's shoulder and neck in rapid succession. Wei Wuxian knew firsthand that while cultivators of the Gusu Lan Sect looked like fragile, ethereal scholars, their physical strength was downright terrifying. A precision strike like that should have paralyzed anyone on the spot. Yet A-Tong didn't even flinch. His left fingers tightened their vise grip, his face twisting into a hideous, purple grimace of agony. Lan Jingyi lunged forward to pry the fingers loose, but the hand might as well have been forged from solid iron; it didn't budge a hair. Within seconds, a sickening snap rang through the room.

A-Tong’s head slumped limply to one side. The fingers finally went slack—his neck snapped clean in two.

Right before their eyes, he had strangled himself to death.

A-Ding backed away, her voice trembling into a shriek. “…A ghost! There’s an invisible ghost in here! It made him choke himself to death!”

Her shrill, terrified wail rattled the rafters, making everyone’s skin crawl, and the terrified onlookers bought it instantly. Wei Wuxian, however, reached the exact opposite conclusion:Not a ghost.

He’d already checked the talismans the disciples had plastered over the room—they were pure spirit-repelling wards, papering the hall so densely not even a breeze could slip through. If an actual vengeful ghost had crossed the threshold, the paper would have instantly burst into spectral green flames instead of hanging completely inert.

The kids weren't slow; the thing hunting them was simply operating on an entirely different level of savagery. The cultivation world had strict metrics for what constituted a "fierce ghost"—a spirit that claimed one victim a month over three consecutive months met the threshold. Wei Wuxian had personally established that classification system back in his prime, and it seemed they were still using it. He was the undisputed master of handling such horrors; by his reckoning, taking a life once every seven days already made an entity exceptionally dangerous. But this thing had butchered three people back-to-back in a matter of minutes. Even a seasoned, celebrated cultivator would sweat trying to formulate a countermeasure on the fly, let alone a squad of wet-behind-the-ears fledglings.

Right as the thought crossed his mind, the torches flickered. A freezing, rancid draft swept through the estate.

In a single breath, every lantern, candle, and torch in both the courtyard and the Eastern Hall went dead.

Darkness dropped like a shroud, and instant hysteria followed. Men and women shoved, clawed, and trampled over one another, screeching in blind panic. Lan Jingyi barked into the pitch-black, “Hold your ground! Do not run! Anyone moving gets pinned down!”

He wasn't bluffing to sound tough. Malevolent entities thrived on chaos and murk; the more people ran and shrieked, the easier it was to become prey without ever seeing the blow coming. Breaking rank in the dark was suicide. But common sense rarely survived pure panic. In seconds, the frantic scuffling bled away, leaving the hall unnervingly hollow—broken only by shallow, ragged breathing and the faint, hitching sobs of the few people too petrified to bolt. There couldn't have been more than a handful left inside.

A sudden flare tore through the shadows. Lan Sizhui had struck a Fire Talisman.

Unlike ordinary flame, the spark of a sacred talisman couldn't be snuffed out by a blast of resentful wind. Holding the burning paper between two fingers, he used it to rekindle the lanterns while the other disciples moved to round up and calm the stragglers. By the warm glow of the firelight, Wei Wuxian casually glanced down at his wrists.

Another cut had vanished.

He froze. Something wasn't adding up.

Originally, he’d had four gashes: two on each wrist. Mo Ziyuan died—first scar gone. Mo Ziyuan’s father dropped—second scar cleared. A-Tong choked himself out—third scar healed. By all counts, three wounds should have sealed, leaving only the deepest, most spite-drenched laceration behind.

Yet his forearms were entirely bare. Not a single trace remained.

Wei Wuxian was dead certain that Madam Mo sat dead-center at the top of Mo Xuanyu’s hit list. That final, jagged cut had unquestionably been carved in her honor. And now it was gone.

Had Mo Xuanyu magically achieved inner peace and forgiven his abusive aunt from the beyond? Impossible. His soul had already been fed to the void as the price of the ritual. The only way that wound could close was if Madam Mo was dead.

Wei Wuxian’s eyes drifted slowly across the room, locking onto Madam Mo. She sat propped up in a chair, surrounded by a couple of weeping servants, her face as bloodless as a corpse's shroud.

Unless she’s already dead.

Wei Wuxian was certain of it now: something had hitched a ride inside her. But if it wasn't a ghostly spirit, what the hell was it?

Suddenly, A-Ding cried out in horror, “His hand… Look at his hand! A-Tong’s left hand is gone!”

Lan Sizhui brought the flaming talisman closer to A-Tong’s body. Sure enough, the wrist ended in a hollow sleeve. The left hand had completely vanished.

Left hand!

A bolt of lightning cracked through Wei Wuxian’s thoughts, stitching every missing piece together in a blinding flash: the rampant butchery, the severed limbs, the vanishing flesh. It was so absurdly obvious he actually burst into a loud snort.

Lan Jingyi snapped, “You utter moron! You can actually laugh right now?!” Then, catching himself, the boy swallowed his own bile—what was the point of picking a fight with the local idiot?

Wei Wuxian caught Lan Jingyi by the sleeve, shaking his head frantically. “No, no, you've got it all wrong!”

Lan Jingyi yanked his arm back in annoyance. “Wrong about what? That you’re not an idiot? Stop making trouble! Nobody has the patience for your nonsense right now!”

Wei Wuxian pointed straight at the twisted corpses of the father and the servant. “Those aren't them!”

Lan Sizhui raised a hand to keep Jingyi from blowing his lid, stepping forward with genuine focus. “What do you mean, ‘those aren't them’?”

Wei Wuxian’s expression turned dead serious. “That thing over there isn't Mo Ziyuan’s dad, and that thing isn't A-Tong.”

Caked in chalky cosmetics, the more solemn he looked, the more utterly deranged he appeared. Yet heard in the flickering gloom of the half-lit hall, his words carried a bone-chilling weight. Lan Sizhui paused, drawn in despite himself. “Why do you say that?”

Wei Wuxian puffed out his chest with ridiculous pride. “The hands! Neither of those two are southpaws. Every time they beat the snot out of me, they always used their right hands. I’d know!”

Lan Jingyi looked ready to spit blood. “Why are you bragging about getting beaten up?! Look at you, strutting around like you won a prize!”

Lan Sizhui, however, broke out in a cold sweat.

He played the past hour back in his head: A-Tong had strangled himself using his left hand. Madam Mo’s husband had shoved his wife to the ground using his left hand.

Yet during the afternoon brawl when Mo Xuanyu was throwing his public fit, both of those men had instinctively grabbed, hauled, and shoved using their right hands. It was unthinkable that both of them had spontaneously turned left-handed right before drawing their last breaths.

Whatever force was orchestrating this massacre, the answer lay in that severed left limb. Lan Sizhui turned the realization over, his gaze drifting back to Wei Wuxian with quiet astonishment.For him to point this out out of nowhere… it feels far too sharp to be a coincidence.

Wei Wuxian merely offered his best idiot smile, fully aware the breadcrumb had been entirely unsubtle. But desperate times called for crude nudges. Fortunately, Lan Sizhui was too well-mannered to interrogate him, deciding that as long as the eccentric young man was trying to help, his intentions were probably clean.

Turning away from the lunatic, Sizhui’s eyes swept past the weeping A-Ding and landed directly on Madam Mo.

His gaze traced down from her face, down the folds of her silk sleeves, to her limp hands resting against her lap. Her right fingers were porcelain-fair and delicate—the soft hands of a pampered matriarch who’d never worked a day of hard labor in her life.

Her left fingers, however, were noticeably longer, thicker, and knobby with muscle. The joints hooked slightly, brimming with suppressed violence.

That wasn't a woman's hand. That was undeniably the hand of a man!

Lan Sizhui’s voice cracked like a whip: “Pin her down!”

The disciples moved like a single shadow, tackling Madam Mo into the chair. Lan Sizhui offered a hasty, polite “Pardon the offense!” as he flipped a yellow talisman into his palm, driving it down toward her forehead. But before the paper could touch her skin, Madam Mo’s left arm bent backward at an impossible, sickening angle, shooting straight for his throat!

To twist a human arm like that without snapping the bone clean through was anatomically impossible. The strike was blindingly fast, her hooked fingers inches from tearing his windpipe open.

“Aiyoh!”

Lan Jingyi threw his entire weight across Lan Sizhui’s chest, taking the brunt of the attack.

A flare of green light erupted the split-second the claw sank into Jingyi’s shoulder. The fabric ignited into bursts of eerie jade fire, forcing the fingers to instantly recoil. Lan Sizhui stumbled back, safe by a hair’s breadth. He turned to thank his martial brother for the heroic tackle, only to find half of Jingyi’s outer robe burned completely to cinders. Stripping the scorched remnants off in an undignified scramble, Jingyi spun around, his face purple with fury.

“Why the hell did you kick me, you lunatic?! Are you trying to get me killed?!”

Wei Wuxian was already crouched in a corner, hands tucked over his ears. “Wasn't me! I didn't kick anyone!”

It was definitely him. The inner lining of Gusu Lan robes was embroidered with defensive warding scripts in matching thread, capable of turning aside fatal blows in a crisis. But against something this vicious, the fabric was a single-use shield. In that split second, booting Jingyi into the trajectory had been the only way to save Sizhui’s neck.

Before Jingyi could unleash another string of curses, Madam Mo crumpled flat onto the floorboards. The flesh on her face withered in real-time, collapsing into a hollow skull shrink-wrapped in dry skin. From her shoulder socket, the alien male arm tore itself free. It dropped to the pavers, the pale fingers flexing and stretching like a brawler rolling his shoulders before a fight, blue veins pulsing with dark, thrumming vitality.

Thiswas the nightmare the Spirit Attraction Flag had lured in.

Dismemberment was one of the most violent ways to die in this world—barely a step up from having one’s body pulverized to ash, and only just. Unlike dust, severed limbs carried a jagged sliver of the deceased’s lingering hatred. Driven by an agonizing instinct to be whole again, the piece would scour the earth for the rest of its corpse so it could finally find peace. If it found them, it might rest—or it might warp into an even greater catastrophe. And if it couldn't locate its missing parts, it would settle for second best.

And what was second best?

Stealing parts from the living.

It would sever a living person’s left arm, fuse itself onto the stump, drink the host’s vitality bone-dry, discard the husk, and move on to the next body—creeping forward one victim at a time until its original corpse was restored.

The moment it grafted onto a vessel, the host died instantly. Yet until the flesh was drained to a husk, the hand could puppet the corpse around like a living marionette. Its first host had been Mo Ziyuan. Its second, the father. When the man had pushed his wife away, Wei Wuxian had assumed it was bitter grief; looking back, that dead-eyed silence hadn't been despair at all. It was the total, hollow stillness of a fresh corpse.

Its third stop was A-Tong. Its fourth was Madam Mo, taken under the cover of darkness when the lanterns blew out. And the moment she hit the floor, the final cut on Wei Wuxian’s wrist had dissolved into nothing.

Seeing their talismans were useless while the robes offered a physical ward, the Lan disciples stripped off their outer garments in unison, hurling the white robes like nets over the crawling limb until it was swaddled in a thick, cloth cocoon. Within heartbeats, the fabric began to scorch, sputtering with ominous green fire. It was a stopgap at best; once the enchanted cloth turned to ash, the claw would break through.

Taking advantage of the chaos, Wei Wuxian slipped out the door and sprinted straight for the Western Courtyard.

A dozen walking corpses stood frozen in the yard, sealed by the disciples' boundary runes. Wei Wuxian skidded to a halt, reared back, and kicked straight through one of the blood-drawn characters, shattering the circle. He clapped his hands twice.

Crack!

The corpses jolted violently, their eyes rolling back into their sockets, snapping awake as though struck by lightning.

Wei Wuxian pointed a finger. “Get up. Shift’s starting!”

He’d never needed elaborate incantations or ritual bells to herd the dead; plain speech worked just fine. The front row of corpses shuffled forward, trembling on stiff legs. But the second they drew within a few paces of him, their knees buckled like terrified children. Dropping flat onto their bellies, they pressed their faces into the dirt.

Wei Wuxian didn't know whether to laugh or cry. He gave two more claps, much softer this time, but it made no difference. These poor stiffs had been born in Mo Village and died in Mo Village; they were country corpses who had never seen the world. Instinct commanded them to obey the summoner, but an overwhelming, primal terror of the monster standing before them pinned them to the earth, whining and shuddering in the dust.

The nastier and more resentful a creature was, the easier Wei Wuxian could handle it. These harmless bottom-feeders simply couldn't handle his raw spiritual pressure, and he had no materials on hand to craft a makeshift flute to dilute the command. Looking back, the green fire in the Eastern Courtyard was already guttering out.

Suddenly, a wicked spark caught in his mind.

Why the hell am I hunting for vicious, spite-choked corpses out here?

There are three fresh ones cooling right inside the parlor!

He darted back to the Eastern Hall. The Lan disciples were down to their last resort, their longswords driven tip-first into the floorboards to create an iron cage around the thrashing hand. They were leaning all their weight onto the hilts, desperate to keep the limb contained, way too busy to notice who was coming and going. Wei Wuxian strode past them into the shadows, seized the collars of Madam Mo and Mo Ziyuan, and barked in a gravelly whisper:

“Wake up!”

A single call to summon the soul back to the flesh!

Their dead eyes snapped wide, rolling back to pure white, and an ear-splitting, blood-freezing screech tore from their throats—the signature wail of an awakened fierce corpse.

Above their shrill shriek, a third body scrambled up on all fours, offering a pathetic, trembling whine to join the chorus: the father.

Loud lungs, plenty of venom. Wei Wuxian gave a satisfied grin. “See that hand out there?”

He flicked his wrist toward the cage. “Tear it to shreds.”

The three corpses shot across the hall like a black hurricane.

The severed arm snapped through an iron sword blade, breaking free of the cage just as the three one-armed horrors crashed down upon it.

Beyond being unable to resist Wei Wuxian’s command, the family carried an all-consuming hatred for the thing that had butchered them, unleashing every drop of their post-mortem malice onto the limb. Leading the slaughter was Madam Mo. Female fierce corpses were notoriously vicious; with her hair flying wild and her sclera veined with crimson, her fingernails sprouted into jagged talons. Foaming at the mouth, her shrieks shook the roof tiles as she tore into the arm. Mo Ziyuan flanked her, gnashing and clawing in tandem, while the father brought up the rear, plugging every gap in the assault.

The young Lan disciples, who had been barely clinging to life moments ago, stood frozen with their mouths hanging open.

They had only ever read about corpse-on-corpse brawls in old records and tavern rumors. Watching limbs, black blood, and rotted sinew tear through the air in person had them completely spellbound. In fact, they couldn't look away. It was… ridiculously awesome.

The battle raged at a fever pitch until Mo Ziyuan let out an agonized howl and stumbled back. The hand had punched straight into his gut, spilling coils of blackened intestines onto the pavers. Madam Mo lost what little sanity she had left, shielding her brat behind her withered frame while swiping with talons that whistled through the air with the force of iron broadswords. Yet Wei Wuxian could see the tide turning.

Even three freshly butchered corpses working in tandem couldn't pin down a single severed arm!

Wei Wuxian’s eyes narrowed. He curled the tip of his tongue against his lip, holding back a piercing whistle. A single sharp note from him would stoke the corpses' bloodlust tenfold, easily turning the tables—but blowing that whistle would instantly give away his identity to anyone with half a brain. In the space of an inhale, the arm struck like a viper, snapping Madam Mo’s neck with brutal, surgical precision.

With the Mo family on the verge of total collapse, Wei Wuxian braced himself to loose the whistle.

Right at that second, two crisp, resonant notes drifted down from the heavens.

Zheng—zheng.

The notes sounded effortless, like a musician idly brushing across zither strings, yet they carried a crystalline purity that swept through the courtyard like a frost-bitten wind whistling through pine needles. The violent tangle of monsters in the yard froze dead in their tracks.

Color rushed back into the pale faces of the Gusu Lan disciples, their exhaustion replaced by pure, blinding awe. Lan Sizhui wiped a streak of grime from his cheek, snapping his head toward the night sky with radiant delight.

“Hanguang-jun!”

The moment those two celestial notes rang out, Wei Wuxian pivoted on his heel and bolted.

A third note pierced the sky, higher, sharper, cutting through the night with a terrifying edge of quiet slaughter. The three fierce corpses recoiled violently, clamping their remaining right hands over their ears. But the Lan Sect’s Rest-Sound was not so easily deflected; after barely two staggering steps, faint cracking sounds echoed from inside their skulls.

The rogue left arm, already worn down by the brutal brawl, dropped heavily against the stone floor. Its fingers twitched weakly, but the limb itself lay entirely paralyzed.

A heartbeat of dead silence gave way to an explosion of wild, tearful cheers from the young disciples. It was the raw, dizzying euphoria of surviving a nightmare. The long, terrifying night was finally over; their clan's greatest shield had arrived. At this point, they didn't care if they got slapped with heavy disciplinary floggings for "unseemly shouting and disgracing clan decorum."

Lan Sizhui waved excitedly toward the moonlight, but his smile faltered as he scanned the yard. He tugged at Jingyi’s charred sleeve. “Wait, where is he?”

Jingyi was still riding the high. “Who? Where’s who?”

“Young Master Mo,” Sizhui murmured.

Jingyi waved a hand dismissively. “Him? Why are you looking for that freak? Probably figured I’d beat him black and blue and took off running.”

Lan Sizhui offered a helpless sigh. Jingyi was as blunt and unobservant as a wooden plank, never reading between the lines. Deciding against pushing it, Sizhui thought to himself:I’ll just report everything about this man to Hanguang-jun when he lands.

Mo Village slept on, oblivious—or perhaps feigning sleep. Even with blood and screams tearing through the Mo estate all night, not a single townsfolk would dare poke their nose out before sunrise. Gossip had its limits; when the screaming started sounding lethal, looking the other way was basic survival.

Back in the hovel, Wei Wuxian used a handful of dirt to frantically scrub every last trace of the sacrificial array off the floor, then vaulted out the window. Of all the cursed coincidences in the world, the reinforcements had to be Lan cultivators—and of all the Lan cultivators breathing, ithadto be Lan Wangji. Out of everyone from his past life, that man had crossed paths with him, fought with him, and traded blows with him more than almost anyone. If he got spotted, he was a dead man walking.

He needed a getaway mount, and fast. Sprinting past an adjoining yard, he spotted an old stone mill hooked to a patchy, spotted donkey lazily chewing on its bit. Seeing a man barreling toward it like a house on fire, the beast paused, cocking its head to give him a slow, incredibly human side-eye.

Wei Wuxian caught the look and was immediately charmed by the pure, unadulterated contempt in the animal’s eyes.

He lunged forward, grabbed the reins, and dragged the stubborn beast toward the gate. The donkey brayed loudly in protest, planting its hooves into the dirt. With a frantic mix of sweet-talking, tugging, and downright bribery, Wei Wuxian finally coaxed the stubborn creature into a trot, clattering out onto the main road just as the first pale light of dawn began to crack the horizon.
